newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton prices rise in India, seen weak in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Cotton prices rise in India, seen weak in Pakistan.

text.p: Cotton prices rose in India on short supply but were seen falling in Pakistan on low demand and fresh arrivals, dealers said on Friday.
Dealers in Karachi said prices moved both ways to end steady in the week to Friday as supply of the new 1997/98 (July-June) crop soared.
Rates were up early in the week on fears that recent heavy monsoon rains might have damaged the new crop and stocks lying in ginning factories, one dealer said.
"Rising supply of fresh arrivals subsided the fears and prices were back to previous levels," the dealer said.
Prices could come off further in the next few sessions amid low demand from spinners and exporters, dealers said .
In the kerb market on Friday, NIAB-78 variety was quoted at 2,225 rupees ($54.78) per maund (37.32 kg) and MNH-93 at 2,250 rupees per maund.
Following are the weekly cotton spot rates in rupees per maund issued by the private Karachi Cotton Association:
Friday Thursday July 17
In India, cotton prices recovered on a shortage of ready stock as arrivals dropped in the local market in the week to Thursday, traders said.
They said the bulk of the cotton crop of the 1996/97 season (October/September), estimated at 17 million bales (one bale is 170 kgs), had already arrived in the market.
"There's a shortage of quality cotton," said a trader. "A bout of fresh buying by mills pushed prices further up."
"Reports of slow progress of monsoon in cotton-producing regions also aided the firm trend," the trader said.
The four-month June-September monsoon arrived after a week's delay and turned weak in the second half of July, traders said.
In the week to Thursday, spot Bengal-deshi rose 65/80 rupees to 1,010/1,080 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) and Punjab saw-ginned gained 25/40 rupees to 1,825/1,880 rupees per maund.
Among Gujarat varieties, Kalyan rose 500 rupees to 14,500/14,800 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) and wagad moved up 400 rupees to 13,100 rupees per candy.
Long-staple Sankar-4 rose 800/1,000 rupees to 18,500/19,000 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) for the average variety and to 20,500/21,500 rupees for the superior variety.
"Looking at the slow progress of monsoon and a dry spell in some cotton-producing regions the 1997/98 crop may be lower than anticipated," said another trader.
"It is too early to predict the new crop but if the dry spell continues then prices will remain firm," he added.
